final_answer: Free thiols allow mild crosslinking by disulfide formation or Michael addition to acrylates, giving in-situ-gelling, mucoadhesive networks under physiological conditions.
note: Evidence PMC9967816 states thiol-modified HA can be crosslinked at physiological conditions through oxidation into disulfide bonds; PMC10023368 states Michael-addition reactions between thiols and acrylates form hydrogels.

final_answer: It cleaves vicinal diols on the sugar rings to generate aldehyde groups for Schiff-base crosslinking, but ring opening also fragments/weakens the chain and can reduce bioactivity.
note: Evidence windows discuss aldehyde crosslinkers, chitosan Schiff bases and Schiff-base self-healing in general, but none describes periodate oxidation of HA, vicinal-diol cleavage, ring opening, or a drawback such as chain weakening or reduced bioactivity.

final_answer: Adipic dihydrazide grafting installs pendant hydrazides, which react with aldehydes (e.g., oxidized HA or aldehyde-bearing polymers) to form hydrazone-crosslinked hydrogels.
note: Evidence PMC6318583 states oxidized HA is cross-linked with adipic acid dihydrazide and that excess ADH functionalizes HA as hydrazide species combined with oxidized HA as aldehyde species; PMC10370027 describes HA-ADH/HA-Ox hydrazone-crosslinked hydrogels.

final_answer: The fraction of disaccharide units (or target groups) bearing the modification; usually quantified by 1H NMR integration, sometimes by colorimetric assays. DS controls crosslink density, stiffness, and degradation rate.
note: Evidence only gives an example (PMC6864629: a derivative with degree of substitution of 4%, characterized by 1H NMR); it does not define DS as a fraction of disaccharide units, mention colorimetric assays, or state that DS controls crosslink density, stiffness or degradation.

final_answer: Carbodiimide activation of carboxyls is most efficient in mildly acidic (MES-buffered) conditions; excess adipic dihydrazide both raises amidation yield and installs hydrazide handles while minimizing HA-HA crosslinking.
note: Evidence PMC6318583 supports only that an excess of ADH was used in carbodiimide functionalization of HA; no window gives the pH 4.5-5.5 range, MES buffering, why acidic pH is efficient, or that excess ADH raises yield / minimizes HA-HA crosslinking.

final_answer: Under alkaline conditions, DVS undergoes Michael addition with HA hydroxyl groups, forming sulfonyl-bis-ethyl ether crosslinks (the chemistry behind early hylan-type gels).
note: No evidence window describes divinyl sulfone reacting with HA hydroxyls or sulfonyl-bis-ethyl crosslinks; the windows concern bis-sulfone protein conjugation, Hylan G-F 20 outcomes, and BDDE (a different crosslinker).

final_answer: Horseradish peroxidase with H2O2 oxidatively couples the tyramine phenols into dityramine crosslinks, giving fast, cytocompatible in-situ gelation whose rate is tuned by H2O2 dose.
note: Evidence PMC9127275 states hydrogels were prepared by enzymatic crosslinking of tyramine-conjugated HA using horseradish peroxidase in the presence of hydrogen peroxide, rapidly formed within seconds under physiological conditions; PMC9048911 reports favorable cytocompatibility of tyramine-modified HA hydrogel.

final_answer: Strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition needs no UV light, photoinitiator, or metal catalyst, so gels form under fully physiological, cell-friendly conditions with spatial uniformity.
note: Evidence PMC9826943 describes an HA hydrogel platform using bioorthogonal strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) that is cytocompatible; PMC6403731 notes click reactions proceed under mild conditions and are used for cell-compatible hydrogels, unlike the UV-driven photo-click chemistry in PMC7111509.

final_answer: Esterifying the carboxyls makes HA water-insoluble and much slower to degrade, processable into films, membranes, and scaffolds that persist for weeks instead of days.
note: Evidence PMC2738906 describes HYAFF as an insoluble polymer obtained by esterification of hyaluronic acid with benzyl alcohol, involving esterification of the carboxyl groups, with good stability to hydrolysis, used as a tissue-engineering scaffold (also PMC10705868 on HYAFF-11 scaffolds).

final_answer: Each oxidation opens a sugar ring and weakens the backbone; excess periodate or long reaction times depolymerize HA (large MW drop) and destroy receptor-binding epitopes.
note: Evidence windows are off-topic (eye-drop aid, chitosan TEMPO oxidation, LYVE-1 binding); none discusses periodate dosing for HA, ring opening, depolymerization/MW drop, or loss of receptor-binding epitopes.

final_answer: Boronate ester bonds between phenylboronic acid groups and diols are dynamic covalent bonds - they break and reform reversibly, so the network re-knits after damage and is shear-thinning/injectable.
note: Evidence PMC12919407 lists boronate ester among dynamic covalent bonds used for injectable hydrogels that are shear-thinning and self-healing; PMC11564514 states dynamic reversible bonds break and spontaneously reform, restoring structural integrity after damage.

final_answer: Gels are viscoelastic solids: the storage modulus G' (elasticity) and loss modulus G'' (viscous flow), and their ratio (tan delta), predict filler lift, cohesivity, and extrusion behavior better than a Newtonian viscosity number.
note: Evidence PMC11360814 lists storage modulus (G'), loss modulus (G''), tangent delta (tan delta) and cohesivity as key filler rheological properties influencing elastic/viscous behavior and injection ease, and notes lift capability depends on G' and cohesivity (PMC3154544).

final_answer: The tendency of the gel to hold together as a single mass rather than dispersing into particles under stress - it affects how the filler integrates in tissue and resists migration.
note: Evidence windows concern HA molecular-mass gel calibration, adipose cell culture on HA gel, and a filler-migration case title; none defines cohesivity or states that it governs holding together, tissue integration or migration resistance.

note: Evidence PMC3432174 states: 'NHS-activated carboxyl groups in HA react with primary amines present in blood and myocardium to form amide bonds', supporting option B (carboxyl).

final_answer: The activated O-acylisourea can rearrange to a stable N-acylurea (dead end) or hydrolyze; NHS (or sulfo-NHS) traps it as an active ester, and acidic pH plus ADH spacers further raise useful yields.
note: Evidence windows concern EDC/NHS collagen materials, filler trial photos and copper/ascorbate radicals; none mentions O-acylisourea, N-acylurea rearrangement, hydrolysis of the activated intermediate, or NHS trapping it as an active ester.

final_answer: Adding hyaluronidase dissolves HA networks specifically; gels are also often built with protease-cleavable peptide crosslinks so cells can remodel them - degradation is a design variable, not an accident.
note: Evidence supports only MMP-degradable peptide crosslinks (PMC4049825); no window mentions hyaluronidase dissolving HA networks, so the draft's main on-demand mechanism is not settled by this pack.

final_answer: Chemically sulfating HA's hydroxyls gives a heparin-like, highly charged derivative with growth-factor-binding and anticoagulant-adjacent properties used in scaffolds and coatings - properties native HA lacks.
note: Evidence shows high-/low-sulfated HA exist and that HA-HS enhances FGF1 reactivity with FGFRs like heparin (PMC8918722), but does not state sulfation of hydroxyls, anticoagulant-adjacent properties, or scaffold/coating uses.

final_answer: Direct dense substitution on carboxyls destroys CD44 binding (the carboxyls are part of receptor recognition) and solubility; spacers and low degrees of substitution preserve targeting and chain behavior.
note: Evidence windows describe a CD44 binding ELISA, cholesteryl-HA nanogel conjugates targeting CD44-positive tumors, and an unrelated rectal-spacer study; none states that direct dense carboxyl substitution destroys CD44 binding/solubility or that spacers/low substitution preserve targeting.
